Qingju · 青桔2021Commercial brief from Qingju (DiDi) · Programme capstone

Connect cycling rewards to the reasons people ride.

Turning an engagement brief into an experience built around discovery, memories and rewards in leisure cycling.

Problem
Qingju wanted its growth system to raise engagement, but tasks, levels, badges and points sat apart, and riders had to dig deep to see their own progress.
Key decisions
I proposed starting from leisure riding, so that rewards follow finding a route, riding it and recording it, instead of a separate task list. I contributed to the research and interviews, and made the problem framing, personas, journey map, user flow and low-fidelity wireframes; as a team we built the high-fidelity proposal on top of them.
Outcome
Our four-person team’s proposal won the Best Proposal Award in the Qingju growth-system track of the Zhiqun China Design Award & Competition. The concept leaned towards a complete game system; a 2026 retrospective at the end cuts it back against three metrics: activation, frequency and retention.

01 · The challenge

Why would a rider care about a growth system?

The brief was to improve Qingju’s growth system with user engagement as the goal. My review of the product at the time found tasks, levels, badges and points separated from one another, with progress and benefits buried in the navigation.

Before designing anything, I broke “active” down: from trial to first rides, habit and advocacy, what to measure at each stage and which threshold counts. The judgement at the time was that commuting demand is relatively fixed, so the extra rides would have to come from leisure time.

I proposed leisure cycling as the research direction. Commuting usually has a fixed destination; parks, greenways and city exploration introduce questions about where to go, what to see and what to remember. This was a scenario hypothesis that shaped the research.

Tobie’s note

Growth should connect to what people want from a ride, rather than remain a number that accumulates after unlocking a bike.

02 · Research

Understand the ride before designing the reward.

We combined interviews, a questionnaire and field observation to explore leisure riders’ behaviour, motivations, sharing habits and awareness of benefits. We interviewed 11 people and collected 128 questionnaire returns, 85 of them valid.

Recurring themes in the interview summaries included discovering unfamiliar places, visiting shops with friends, and recording or sharing a ride. In the questionnaire, about nine in ten had not noticed the growth system. I contributed to the early research and interviews, then translated these themes into personas and journeys.

03 · Synthesis

Map the opportunities before, during and after a ride.

A list of needs—exploration, social connection, memories—was not enough to guide the interface. Through user modelling and journey maps, I connected them to specific moments: choosing a route, pausing along the way and reflecting afterwards.

Before

Make choosing easier

Help people find places and routes that match their interests, reducing the effort of planning in an unfamiliar area.

During

Leave room to explore

Connect the experience to places along the route and progress through the ride.

After

Make the ride memorable

Connect memories, rewards and sharing so the experience has value beyond the journey itself.

04 · Design decision

Let rewards follow the experience.

Between personas and proposal there was a filtering step. I wrote a point-of-view statement for each of the three rider types and turned each into a “how might we” question. Ideas from brainstorming were assessed on novelty, usefulness, feasibility and relevance, leaving five directions: a treasure map, treasure chests, route discussions, ride memories and simpler recording. Finally we placed them into entry, mechanism and outcome so that they formed one system.

We did not treat another points-and-badges system as the only answer. Instead, we connected route discovery, ride records and growth benefits in one path. The ride itself provides value first; rewards make sense within that experience.

Before wireframing, I drew the whole path as a flow chart to settle where rewards, the vault and ride memories attach once a ride ends. My low-fidelity work translated the opportunities into screens and flows for route selection, ride records, rewards and sharing. It gave the team a concrete basis for discussing entry points and task order before the final visual design.

05 · Trade-offs

A rich concept still needs boundaries.

Connecting routes, shops and rewards creates a more complete experience, but also brings content, partnership and operational costs. We did not include every interesting idea in the first proposal; we organised it around the core journey before and after riding.

Looking back, I would validate a smaller loop first: can someone find a route they want to ride, complete it, and understand the relationship between the ride record and its reward? Wider partnerships should follow evidence that this loop works.

06 · Outcome & reflection

From a business goal to a concrete experience proposal.

The project produced a research synthesis, personas and journeys, wireframe flows, and a team high-fidelity proposal. My central contribution was proposing the leisure-cycling direction and carrying research themes into concrete flows.

The proposal received the Best Proposal Award in the Qingju growth-system track of the Zhiqun China Design Award & Competition, as the joint work of a four-person team.

As a next step, I would observe whether riders can independently understand and complete the proposed journey.

07 · Looking back in 2026

If I did it today: decide the metrics, then the rewards.

The 2021 deck had already broken “active” down once, into four stages (trial, first rides, habit, advocacy), each with a threshold. Today I would go one step further and reduce it to three numbers that can be read directly: activation (a first ride started from a route entry point), frequency (rides per week) and retention (riding again within 30 days). Each 2021 touchpoint then has a place: the home banner, treasure map and route discussions serve activation; post-ride coins, chests and shop coupons serve frequency; ride memories and scenery cards serve retention. Seen this way, frequency rested almost entirely on the treasure-chest numbers.

I would keep two things: rewards settled after the ride, rather than a separate task list; and ride memories, which turn a ride into something worth revisiting. I would cut the chest upgrades. Gold, silver and bronze chests were upgraded with coins to raise drop rates, but we never modelled coin issuance, coupon cost or drop rates. Numbers without an economic model are hard to tune once live, and harder to withdraw.

The first experiment I would run answers one question: when should the reward arrive? Users are randomised into two groups. Group A gets the reward the moment the bike is locked; group B gets it batched and delivered later. The primary metric is the 7-day repeat-ride rate, with reward cost per repeat ride as a guardrail. “Rewards should sit right next to the ride” was an assumption of the 2021 proposal, and it was never tested.

Looking back, what the project lacked most was a test with users: the wireframe flow was only tested within the team and never tried by riders.

Tobie’s note

Name the number you will watch before designing the reward; otherwise there is nothing to judge it against.
